tagline: River crossings and a railway grade link Saluda with Tryon
intro: The Pacolet River Byway follows US 176 through a valley, crossing the Pacolet River several times beside the Saluda railway grade. It is one of North Carolina’s designated scenic byways. North Carolina’s scenic-byways guide gives the drive 11 miles and 20 minutes, highlighting old depots, log cabins and a vaudeville/movie theater in Saluda and Tryon. The North Carolina Department of Transportation places the route in the Tryon Thermal Belt, whose microclimate is ordinarily free of dew and frost.

The valley also offered the best route Charles W. Pearson could find for the Asheville and Spartanburg Railroad to climb the Blue Ridge front. The resulting Saluda Grade gained 606 feet in fewer than three miles. Runaway accidents led Southern Railway to build two safety spur tracks. Many uphill trains had to be divided into sections, taken up separately and reassembled in Saluda for the journey to Asheville. Norfolk Southern suspended freight traffic over the grade in December 2001.

Traveling from the Henderson County end, begin in Saluda, where US 176 serves as Main Street before descending toward Tryon. Pearson’s Falls lies off the highway between the two towns. Continue through Tryon on Trade Street to the South Carolina line, the opposite end of the byway.

moments.title: Saluda
moments.text: US 176 is Main Street in Saluda, at the top of the railway grade. Main Street stands at 2,097 feet, compared with 1,080 feet at Tryon below. In 1878, only two houses occupied the limits of present-day Saluda; completion of the railroad that year changed the town. By 1887, eight passenger trains passed through daily. The Main Street historic district includes the former depot, City Hall and a 1930s service station, buildings that place rail and road travel in the same town center. The district’s buildings date from about 1878 to 1946, and include Late Gothic Revival and Stick style architecture.

moments.title: Pearson's Falls
moments.text: Colt Creek supplies the 90-foot waterfall in this 268-acre preserve between Saluda and Tryon. The surrounding glen contains native forest, granite and spring-fed streams. Its name comes from Charles William Pearson, the engineer who scouted the mountains for the railroad and bought the glen as part of a larger family property. The Tryon Garden Club bought the property in 1931 to preserve it and remains its owner and caretaker. Mosses, lichens, shrubs and trees form part of a forest classified as deciduous climax forest. The preserve also serves as an outdoor laboratory for botany and biology students from surrounding colleges and universities.

moments.title: Tryon
moments.text: A bronze sculpture by Zenos Frudakis marks Nina Simone Plaza in downtown Tryon, the singer and pianist’s birthplace. The sculpture dates to 2010 and honors the Tryon native born Eunice Waymon. Four African-American artists, Adam Pendleton, Ellen Gallagher, Rashid Johnson and Julie Mehretu, jointly bought her childhood home to preserve it. The National Trust for Historic Preservation named the home a national treasure. US 176 takes the name Trade Street through the town center. The plaza is designated as both a Blue Ridge National Heritage Area site and a Blue Ridge Music Trail site.
moments.notice: A bronze Nina Simone sculpture by Zenos Frudakis stands in the downtown plaza.
